newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu to head home Friday, urges truce.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to head home Friday, urges truce.

text.p: Zaire's ailing and embattled president, Mobutu Sese Seko, planned to return home from France on Friday to confront the growing support for rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
In a statement on the eve of his departure, Mobutu called for a truce in his strife-torn nation and the creation of a national council to find a solution to the five-month-old crisis.

The council would bring together Zaire's different currents of opinion, the army and parliament to find "appropriate ways" out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exception", he said in the statement, issued in France.

As the rebels insisted that only face-to-face talks between Kabila and Mobutu would halt the fighting, France advised its nationals to leave Zaire and sent troops and aircraft to nearby Congo and Gabon to protect them if need be.

Zaire's main opposition group, the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) of veteran radical Etienne Tshisekedi, said it shared Kabila's aim of toppling Mobutu, 66, and had sent envoys to talk to him.

Mobutu's son Nzanga said his father did not rule out talks with the rebels, saying: "He is going to the capital tomorrow. His intention is to find a solution to the present crisis in consultation with parliament, the government and the military high command."
Prime Minister Kenga wa Dondo, under fire for his handling of the war, returned home from Kenya, where he backed a regional call for a truce and talks.
While he was away, the transitional parliament voted to sack him in a vote rejected by his supporters as invalid.
"He said when he arrived at midday that he is still prime minister until further notice," one source close to Kengo said.
In Lubumbashi, the leader of the biggest party in Zaire's autonomy-hungry mining province of Shaba said nothing would stop Kabila's rebels taking the province if the war went on.
Kyungu wa Kumwanza, Shaba's suspended governor, called on Mobutu to meet Kabila for talks but said they must also include regional leaders such as himself.
"The truth is, all the people here are waiting eagerly for Mr Kabila. They see him as a saviour," Kyungu said.
Kenya's foreign minister, Laurent Kabila, said U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would fly to rebel-held eastern Zaire on Friday to meet Kabila and press him to support a ceasefire.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in Cape Town that if a ceasefire could be brokered in Zaire the Security Council might send troops to bolster the peace.

The rebels took up arms in October in a dispute about Zairean nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority, who form the core of Kabila's fighting force. An alliance of anti-Mobutu groups rallied around the cause.

Kabila's popularity increased dramatically as his forces notched up victory after victory. Residents of Kinshasa's poor districts, Tshisekedi's power base, openly welcome the prospect of his arrival in the capital.
Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August and has since spent most of his time in Europe, left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after fresh treatment.
Tshisekedi's supporters want their leader appointed prime minister in place of Kengo and they say Mobutu, who has ruled since seizing power in 1965, should endorse the move.
